title: Word-for-Word Literal Translation Trap
description: Candidates idiom ke individual shabdon ka literal Hindi translation dhoondhte hain aur physical action wale option ko tick kar dete hain.
incorrectExample: *"The clerk spilled the beans" -> Interpreting as 'Dropping food grains or vegetables on the floor'.
correctExample: "The clerk spilled the beans" = Disclosed confidential information prematurely.
whyWrong: Idiom non-compositional hota hai; uske shabdon ka physical dictionary meaning idiom ke metaphorical meaning se poori tarah alag hota hai.
ruleAnchor: Rule RC-01: Literal vs Figurative Meaning Filter.

title: Single-Word Synonym Attraction Trap
description: Option mein idiom ke kisi ek word ka synonym dekh kar candidate use sahi samajh baithta hai, bina poore phrase ke figurative sense ko samjhe.
incorrectExample: *"Burn the midnight oil" -> Selecting 'Combustion of kerosene or fossil fuel at night'.
correctExample: "Burn the midnight oil" = Working or studying late into the night.
whyWrong: 'Oil' ya 'burn' ka physical synonym dekh kar tick karna trap hai. Idiom poora milkar 'late night study' convey karta hai.
ruleAnchor: Rule RC-01: Literal vs Figurative Meaning Filter.

title: Ignoring Sentence Context Clues
description: Sentence ke surrounding clauses aur tone ko nazarandaz karke seedhe idiom ka generic definition lagana chahte hain chahe context contradict kare.
incorrectExample: *"Despite intense hostility, the candidate kept his cool" -> Choosing 'Felt physically cold'.
correctExample: "Kept his cool" = Maintained emotional composure and self-control.
whyWrong: 'Despite intense hostility' ek clear emotional context clue hai jo prove karta hai ki yahan psychological composure ki baat ho rahi hai.
ruleAnchor: Rule RC-02: Sentence Context Isolation Protocol.

title: Confusing Lookalike Idioms: 'Break the ice' vs 'Bury the hatchet'
description: Dono idioms shanti ya baatcheet se jude hain, lekin unke target participants bilkul alag hain.
incorrectExample: *"The long-standing warring factions broke the ice" -> Confusing strangers with bitter adversaries.
correctExample: "Warring factions buried the hatchet" (Peace after feud); "Strangers broke the ice" (Social awkwardness removed).
whyWrong: 'Break the ice' strangers ke beech initial awkwardness todta hai; 'bury the hatchet' dushmano ke beech purani ladai khatam karta hai.
ruleAnchor: Rule RC-03: Distinguishing Confusing Lookalike Idioms.

title: Disclosure vs Rumour: 'Spill the beans' vs 'Hear through grapevine'
description: Candidates secret batane (active disclosure) aur afwah sunne (passive gossip reception) ko interchange kar dete hain.
incorrectExample: *Saying an auditor 'heard through grapevine' when he was the confidential whistleblower who confessed.
correctExample: Insider reveals = 'Spilled the beans'; Outsider receives gossip = 'Heard through the grapevine'.
whyWrong: 'Spill the beans' insider ka act hai; 'grapevine' informal third-party rumors ko receive karne ka channel hai.
ruleAnchor: Rule RC-12: Disclosure vs Rumour Disambiguation.

title: Working Late vs Working Under Pressure: 'Midnight oil' vs 'Against the clock'
description: Dono expressions mehnat darshate hain, lekin unke core constraints (night hours vs imminent deadline) alag hote hain.
incorrectExample: *Describing a race against a 5 PM deadline as 'burning the midnight oil' during broad daylight.
correctExample: Broad daylight race against a 5 PM deadline = 'Working against the clock'; Studying till 3 AM = 'Burning the midnight oil'.
whyWrong: 'Midnight oil' der raat ke ghanton par focus karta hai; 'against the clock' deadline beat karne ki tezi par.
ruleAnchor: Rule RC-10: Time & Frequency Boundary Precision.

title: Premature Action vs Calculated Risk: 'Jump the gun' vs 'Take the plunge'
description: Bina soche waqt se pehle galat kadam uthana (jump gun) aur soch-samajh kar bada faisla lena (take plunge) alag-alag hain.
incorrectExample: *Praising an entrepreneur for 'jumping the gun' when they took a well-planned bold risk.
correctExample: Well-planned bold commitment = 'Took the plunge'; Acting hastily before permission = 'Jumped the gun'.
whyWrong: 'Jump the gun' negative blunder hai (premature mistake); 'take the plunge' deliberate courage hai.
ruleAnchor: Rule RC-03: Distinguishing Confusing Lookalike Idioms.

title: Financial Hardship vs Expensive Price: 'Hand to mouth' vs 'Arm and a leg'
description: Vastu ki unchi keemat aur vyakti ki garibi ke beech grammar aur context mismatch create karna.
incorrectExample: *"The high-speed network server lives from hand to mouth."
correctExample: "The high-speed server costs an arm and a leg"; "The impoverished laborer lives from hand to mouth."
whyWrong: Commodity 'costs an arm and a leg'; insaan ya pariwar 'lives from hand to mouth'. Dono ke subjects interchange nahi ho sakte.
ruleAnchor: Rule RC-11: Financial & Resource Context Precision.

title: Reconciliation vs Mere Agreement: 'Bury the hatchet' vs 'See eye to eye'
description: Dushmani ke baad shanti sthapit karna aur kisi aam mudde par sahmat hona dono alag-alag situations hain.
incorrectExample: *Using 'buried the hatchet' when colleagues simply agreed on tomorrow's lunch venue.
correctExample: "They see eye to eye on the lunch venue"; "After years of bitter litigation, the brothers buried the hatchet."
whyWrong: 'Bury the hatchet' ke liye purana hostility/feud hona mandatory prerequisite hai.
ruleAnchor: Rule RC-13: Reconciliation vs Simple Agreement.

title: Fixed Expression Distortion: Changing Articles or Nouns
description: Sentence correction questions mein examiner idiom ke article ya plural noun ko alter kar deta hai.
incorrectExample: *"To put it in the nutshell..." or *"He spilled the bean."
correctExample: "To put it in a nutshell..." (article 'a'); "He spilled the beans" (plural 'beans').
whyWrong: Idiom ke articles ('a' vs 'the') aur noun numbers (singular vs plural) historically frozen hote hain.
ruleAnchor: Rule RC-04: Fixed Phraseology & Non-Substitution Law.

title: Possessive Form Discord in 'One's' Idioms
description: Template form 'one's' ko subject ke pronoun se match na karna aur ungrammatical sentence banana.
incorrectExample: *"The judge lost one's temper during the proceedings."
correctExample: "The judge lost his (or her) temper during the proceedings."
whyWrong: 'One's' sirf tab rehta hai jab subject khud indefinite pronoun 'one' ho ('One must keep one's word'). Otherwise subject se agree karega.
ruleAnchor: Rule RC-05: Subject-Possessive Concord Rule in Idioms.

title: Treating Idioms and Proverbs as Identical Categories
description: Candidates proverbs (kahawat) aur idioms (muhavare) ke syntactic aur functional difference ko bhool jate hain.
incorrectExample: *Classifying 'A stitch in time saves nine' as a verbal idiom.
correctExample: "A stitch in time saves nine" = Proverb (independent sentence of wisdom); "Bite the bullet" = Idiom (phrase).
whyWrong: Proverb poora independent moral sentence hota hai; idiom sentence ka ek phrase constituent hota hai.
ruleAnchor: Rule RC-06: Idiom vs Proverb Structural Demarcation.

title: Confusing Phrasal Verbs with Full Idioms
description: Verb + Particle combination (phrasal verb) ko full idiomatic phrase ke sath confuse kar dena.
incorrectExample: *Treating 'call off' as a multi-word noun idiom.
correctExample: "Call off" = Phrasal Verb (verb + particle = cancel); "In black and white" = Idiom (adverbial phrase = in writing).
whyWrong: Phrasal verbs strictly verb syntax follow karte hain; idioms nouns, adjectives aur prepositional clauses encompass karte hain.
ruleAnchor: Rule RC-07: Idiom vs Phrasal Verb Grammatical Boundary.

title: Emotional Tone Contradiction in Sentence Completion
description: Sentence negative setback describe kar raha hai, lekin candidate positive celebration idiom insert kar deta hai.
incorrectExample: *"After receiving the termination notice, Mohan was on cloud nine."
correctExample: "After receiving the termination notice, Mohan was down in the dumps."
whyWrong: Sentence ki logical polarity negative hai, isliye positive emotion ('on cloud nine') severe logical contradiction banata hai.
ruleAnchor: Rule RC-08: Idiom Sentence Completion Strategy.

title: Over-interpreting Literal Sentences as Idiomatic
description: Sentence sach mein physical event describe kar raha hai, par candidate zabardasti metaphorical meaning impose kar deta hai.
incorrectExample: *Interpreting "The gardener pulled up the weeds" as an idiom about removing corrupt employees.
correctExample: When the context is a physical garden, the words are literal; do not force an idiom where none exists.
whyWrong: Agar sentence ka literal physical meaning poori tarah fit aur logical hai, toh zabardasti metaphorical meaning nahi lagaya jata.
ruleAnchor: Rule RC-01: Literal vs Figurative Meaning Filter.

title: Misinterpreting 'Bite the bullet' as Aggressive Rather Than Enduring
description: 'Bullet' shabd dekh kar candidate sochta hai ki yeh violent attack ya aggression ke liye hai.
incorrectExample: *Interpreting 'Bite the bullet' as 'Opening fire on enemies' or 'Displaying aggressive anger'.
correctExample: "Bite the bullet" = Forcing oneself to endure an inevitable, painful, or unpleasant task with courage.
whyWrong: Historical root anesthesia ke bina bullet chabane se hai; iska sense pain ko stoically jhelna hai, kisi par attack karna nahi.
ruleAnchor: Rule RC-01: Literal vs Figurative Meaning Filter.

title: Misinterpreting 'A blessing in disguise' as Deceitful Imposter
description: 'Disguise' (bhesh badalna) dekh kar candidate use dhokha ('wolf in sheep's clothing') samajh baithta hai.
incorrectExample: *Interpreting 'A blessing in disguise' as 'A treacherous enemy pretending to be a friend'.
correctExample: "A blessing in disguise" = An apparent misfortune that ultimately brings wonderful unexpected advantages.
whyWrong: Yeh positive outcome hai jo shuru mein bura lagta tha; 'wolf in sheep's clothing' negative dhokha hai.
ruleAnchor: Rule RC-09: Emotion & Psychological Tone Alignment.

title: Inventing Imaginary Idioms via Direct Hindi Calque
description: Hindi muhavaron ka word-for-word English translation banakar sochna ki yeh valid English idiom hai.
incorrectExample: *Translating 'Naach na jaane aangan tedha' literally into '*If you can't dance, the courtyard is crooked*'.
correctExample: The actual English idiom is: "A bad workman always blames his tools."
whyWrong: English idioms English culture aur literature se aate hain; Hindi muhavaron ka word-to-word translation English mein nonsense hota hai.
ruleAnchor: Rule RC-04: Fixed Phraseology & Non-Substitution Law.
